stories.title: Solar eclipse 2026: Africa witnesses partial eclipse
stories.summary: Part of the world turned its eyes to the skies this Wednesday. The eclipse was also visible across Africa. In Tabarka, where the phenomenon was most pronounced in Tunisia, 59.06% of the Sun was obscured. The partial eclipse was also visible from Dakar and several regions of Senegal, with a maximum of around 37% of the Sun's disk obscured towards the end of the day. And to make sure they didn't miss the celestial event, our correspondents in Tunisia and Senegal also put on their special eclipse glasses.

stories.title: Russia-Ukraine war: Grain hub attacks raise fears over global food prices
stories.summary: Kyiv and Moscow have been trading attacks on each other's grain warehouses, as concerns mount that global food prices could rise as a result. Russia struck Ukraine's largest grain shipment port on the Danube overnight, causing damage and setting off a fire. The attack came a day after Ukraine hit Novorossiysk, a major grain hub in Russia's part of the Black Sea.

stories.title: European drought shrivels crops despite farmers’ best efforts to adapt
stories.summary: The drought roasting much of Europe this summer is taking a heavy toll on crops across the continent, from potatoes in the Netherlands to corn in Bosnia. Triodos, a Dutch bank with a focus on sustainability, has warned that this could reduce gross domestic product across the EU by 1 percent for 2026 – or around €180 billion.

stories.title: Lagos: Electric vehicles offer an alternative as fuel prices soar
stories.summary: If you know Nigeria's city of Lagos, you're surely familiar with the hum of its traffic jams. But a new sound is emerging... or rather, one is disappearing. As soaring fuel prices have hit Nigeria in recent years, some motorists are turning to electric vehicles. But in Africa's biggest oil producer, the transition remains fraught with challenges.

stories.title: Air India to test all pilots for banned substances
stories.summary: It comes after one of its planes suddenly lost altitude last week, with a number of passengers injured.
stories.post: 📰 NEWS: Air India to test all pilots for banned substances. It comes after one of its planes suddenly lost altitude last week, with a number of passengers injured. Source: BBC World.
article_sentences: Air India is to test all of its pilots for banned substances, starting immediately.
It comes after an incident last week in which its Phuket to Delhi flight suddenly lost altitude, with a preliminary report saying the senior pilot had to retake their substance test.
Reports say they had tested positive for marijuana.
Pilots at the airline's budget arm, Air India Express, will also be subject to the tests from Thursday.
Existing rules require at least 10% of pilots to be tested at random.
Seventeen passengers and crew were injured when the Airbus lost about 91 metres (300 feet) in height shortly after departure on 4 August.
It is being investigated by Indian authorities working alongside Airbus and France's air safety agency.
Both pilots of the flight have been removed from duties until the investigation is complete.
In a memo seen by the BBC, Air India said it was "important to go further" in its testing.

"This initiative, which goes beyond regulatory requirements, reflects our determination to uphold the highest standards of safety and professionalism, and to provide reassurance to our passengers, stakeholders and the community at large," it said.
The airline has already been under scrutiny after a June 2025 flight from Ahmedabad to London crashed shortly after take-off, killing 241 people on board and 19 on the ground.
Only one passenger survived.

stories.title: Crowds reflect on watching 'incredible' eclipse
stories.summary: People headed to beaches, parks and hills in their droves to catch the rare event.
stories.post: 📰 NEWS: Crowds reflect on watching 'incredible' eclipse. People headed to beaches, parks and hills in their droves to catch the rare event. Source: BBC Science.
article_sentences: Eclipse watchers gathered on beaches, hilltops and parks to watch the Moon pass in front of the Sun on Wednesday, describing the rare event as "incredible".
People across Kent, Surrey and Sussex brought out solar glasses and improvised pinhole cameras with kitchen colanders to watch the celestial event.
Many turned the occasion into a picnic or party in the sun as temperatures climbed into the 30s.
Between 18:20 and 20:10 BST, the Moon caused a near-total eclipse of the Sun, giving people across the UK their best chance to witness the phenomenon since 1999.
Cars queued on coastal roads as eclipse enthusiasts gathered on beaches from Whitstable to Goring-by-Sea.
Spectators also flocked to the South Downs, and people turned up to witness the moment at beauty spots from Tunbridge Wells Common in Kent to Ockham Common in Surrey.
Rhiannon Quinche, from Tunbridge Wells, said it was "amazing" and the "strangest thing ever".

She said: "It was like everything kind of went dark and it's just like this really eerie light, and even the birds don't know what's happening, it's so amazing, this little line of sun, I've not seen anything like it before."
In Eastbourne, Michael Simpson watched the eclipse with his daughter Chloe, and his sister, Anne.
He was in Nigeria when the 1999 solar eclipse happened, but it was the rainy season and there wasn't much to see, although he did notice the birds "took off".
Watching this year's eclipse from the UK, he said it was "amazing".
He said you could feel the temperature dropping and the light getting dimmer, before what looked like a crescent moon appeared, except it was a "crescent sun".
